en: Homage to the glorious Vajraḍāka!

Having prostrated to him who is seated upon a corpse, who has three eyes and faces turned in all directions, and who—along with Vārāhī of crimson limbs—is trampling the Lord of Nagas with his feet while holding her with two primary arms and him with the other two; |||

With the remaining [four] left hands he holds a sword, a noose, a human head, and a goat's head; and with the four right hands he bears a knife, a trident, an axe, and a ḍamaru drum—this is the one named Saṃvara. || 1 ||
Just as it was stated word by word in each tantra by the Lion of the Śākyas,
I have therefore extracted it in its entirety and composed it for my own sake.
Facing east and northeast, one should know that according to the Yoginīmata, the cremation ground (śmaśāna) is located in all directions and intermediate points, as well as to the left and right.
In the eastern cremation ground, Caṇḍogra, there is a great tree, a śirīṣa.
There also resides Śakra, mounted upon Airāvata, fair-complexioned, wielding a vajra and holding a skull-cup.
Vāsuki, the king of the nāgas, white in color and bearing the mark of a blue lotus, stood at the forefront of the Lord, bowing with his palms joined in reverence. || 5 ||
In the north is the Gahvara Aśvattha tree; there dwells Kuvera, who is carried by men, and who holds a white skull-cup while vomiting forth a jewel.
There was the Naga Takṣaka, resembling a bandhūka flower;
though marked with a svastika upon his hood, he remained bowed with his head in a gesture of joined palms.
In the western direction is the Aśoka tree; [the deity there] is white, holding a skull filled with flames, possessing seven nooses, seated upon a crocodile, and bearing a skull-cup.
And Karkoṭaka, the lord of serpents, possessing a luster dark like the color of dūrvā grass,
bears three lines upon his neck and stands with his head bowed and palms joined in reverence.
In the south is Vibhīṣaṇa, who is of the color of a mango tree; Yama is mounted upon a buffalo, black in color, with red eyes, stout, fierce, holding a staff and a skull-cup.
And the lord of serpents named Padma, white in color and marked on his head with a drop of vermilion, requested permission from the Teacher with his palms joined in reverence. (11)
In the northeast is the great Nyagrodha tree, where Aṭaṭṭahāsa resides;
he is white, holds a trident and a skull, is the Lord of Kapālī, dwells in a cow-pen, and is clothed in a tiger skin.
The lord of serpents, Mahāpadma, also possesses a luster equal to the light of the moon;
he bears the mark of a trident upon his hood, with his head bowed in a gesture of joined palms.
In the south (Lakṣmī’s direction) is Karañja, and Agni is in the southeast;
Kharva is at the bone [corner], and Rakta is in the southeast, holding a skull-bowl filled with blood, along with a rosary and a water-pot.
Resembling the throat of a peacock, Ananta has a lotus as his emblem upon his head;
with palms joined in reverence, he bows while stationed at the feet of the Lord.
In the southwest is Nirṛti, blue in color, seated upon a corpse, holding a sword and a skull-cup;
he is naked, known as Ghorāndhakāra (Dreadful Darkness), and has a garland of human skulls upon his head. || 16 ||
Marked with a half-moon on his hood and having smoke-colored spots on his fingers,
the king of serpents sits upon the matted locks of Laṭā with his palms joined in reverence at his head.

In the northwest is Arjuna, whose tree is the Śākhin; he is smoke-colored, seated upon a deer, possesses a yellow banner, holds a skull-bowl, and stands amidst the sound of "kila-kila" cries. || 18 ||
Śaṅkha, Kalaṅkita, Gaura, Puṭa, Añjali, and Asaṣṭama—these eight lords of serpents stood there, adorned with ornaments. (19)
Indra and the others, the eight guardians of the directions and time, together with their consorts, have four arms;
with two hands they hold their palms joined in reverence, and with the remaining two they bear their respective emblems. (20)
Ghana, Jayabhadra, Śrīnanda, Vṛṣṭisupriya, Drutaghoṣa, Caṇḍa, Varṣa, Purāṇa, and Cāpala; || 21 ||
Those eight terrifying clouds stood in the eight cremation grounds;
some produced the sounds of lightning and rained down torrents of water.
And the night-roaming Rākṣasas of cruel form, who sleep during the day and reside in their seats, stood upon the trees devouring the flesh of men. (23)
On every side, all around these great trees, there stood lovely secondary trees, endowed with branches, flowers, and fruits. || 24 ||
With the cries of dogs, jackals, lions, tigers, goats, and boars;
with cats, sheep, wolves, and birds such as crows and owls on the left; || 25 ||
It was filled with Piśācas who were like corpses, hanging from hooks, pierced by spikes, possessing only skeletons or half-remaining skulls, and with their bodies half-burnt on funeral pyres.

With perfected ones (siddhas) offering oblations, with divine assemblies of yoginīs, with ritual knives, skull-cups, and khaṭvāṅga staffs, and with sacrificial fires and sealed offerings of food. || 27 ||
Adorned with white shrines, cremation grounds, and so forth, and possessing the eight siddhis, the Ḍāka stands there in the center among the Yoginīs for the welfare of the world. (28)
... (lacuna) ...
seized.
Whatever merit I have obtained this very day by performing the funeral rites for my own sake, by that may the world attain liberation.
The ritual for the cremation ground is completed. This is the work of the venerable Lūyīpāda.
